title: Non-rotating black holes
one_line_summary: Opens Part D by learning to read the Schwarzschild vacuum geometry for all r: it asks what coordinates mean, separates the removable r = 2m singularity from the curvature singularity at r = 0, maps light-cone structure with spacetime diagrams, removes the horizon problem with Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, and then describes event horizons, collapse, tides, the Newtonian dark-star analogue, observational evidence and theoretical doubts.
role_in_book: Chapter 15 derived the Schwarzschild metric as the field outside a star and Chapter 16 tested it in the weak field, always with r well above 2m. Chapter 17 is the first chapter of Part D and takes the same metric away from any source, so the reader must confront coordinate artefacts, horizons and singularities. It supplies the tools used throughout the rest of the part: classifying coordinates by the inverse metric, light-cone diagrams, analytic extension between coordinate patches, and the idea of an absolute horizon. The misleading Schwarzschild-coordinate picture and the pair of black-hole and white-hole extensions set up the maximal (Kruskal) extension and conformal diagrams of Chapter 18, while the closing survey of objections points ahead to charged and rotating holes (Chapters 19-20), the singularity theorems (§20.13) and gravitational-wave detections (Chapter 21).

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why a coordinate label such as x'^0 carries no automatic meaning as time, and can decide whether each coordinate of a given metric is timelike, null or spacelike from the sign of the corresponding diagonal component of the inverse metric.

Reader can justify why Schwarzschild's (t, r, theta, phi) are canonical: t is the static world time, r is the areal radius (spheres of area 4 pi r^2), and theta, phi are fixed by spherical symmetry up to rotation.
Reader can distinguish a coordinate (removable) singularity from a curvature singularity, using the polar axis and the Kretschmann scalar 48 m^2/r^6 as test cases.
Reader can describe what happens to the character of t and r inside r = 2m and why an observer there cannot remain at fixed r.
Reader can derive the radial null geodesics of Schwarzschild in the form t = +/-(r + 2m ln|r - 2m|) + const and sketch the resulting light-cone diagram, including the tipping of cones in region II.

Reader can compute the proper time and the Schwarzschild coordinate time for radial infall from rest at infinity, show the proper time is finite and Newtonian in form, and show that coordinate time diverges logarithmically with r - 2m decaying like exp(-t/2m).
Reader can transform the Schwarzschild metric to advanced Eddington-Finkelstein form (17.22) and to the null-coordinate form (17.24), and explain why the new metric is regular on 0 < r < infinity.

Reader can articulate the logic of an analytic extension: two metrics, their maximal regular domains, and an isometry on the overlap; and can explain why the advanced and retarded versions give different extensions (black hole versus white hole).
Reader can define an event horizon, explain why r = 2m is a one-way null membrane, and contrast this absolute horizon with the observer-dependent horizon of uniform acceleration.
Reader can narrate spherical collapse on an Eddington-Finkelstein diagram, including the growing interval between received signals and the rapid fading of the star.
Reader can reproduce the Newtonian escape-velocity argument giving R = 2GM/c^2 and state what it does and does not capture.
Reader can obtain the radial stretching (+2m/r^3) and transverse squeezing (-m/r^3) tidal accelerations from geodesic deviation and apply them to an infalling astronaut.

Reader can summarize the main lines of evidence for black holes (X-ray binaries, gravitational waves, stellar orbits at the Galactic Centre, horizon-scale imaging) and the main theoretical caveats (symmetry, singularity theorems, interior matching, quantum effects), including why large black holes have low mean density.

teaching_approach.summary: A careful, coordinate-sceptical chapter that treats the Schwarzschild metric as an object to be interpreted rather than a formula to be used. The authors first build diagnostic tools (character of coordinates, invariant tests for singularities, light-cone diagrams), then show how a naive diagram in Schwarzschild coordinates misleads, fix it by designing coordinates in which ingoing light rays are straight, and only then introduce the physical vocabulary of horizons, black holes and white holes. The last third changes register to a qualitative survey: a Newtonian analogue, tidal forces, observational evidence, and a candid list of theoretical objections.
narrative_arc: Motivating worry: once any coordinate transformation is allowed, what, if anything, do the coordinates of a solution mean?
Tool 1: the level surfaces of a coordinate have a causal character read off from g^(a)(a); apply it to show Schwarzschild coordinates are canonical and adapted to the symmetries.
Tool 2: coordinate patches can fail; distinguish removable singularities (polar axis, r = 2m) from a real one (r = 0) by a curvature scalar.
Abstract the metric from its stellar source and notice that r = 2m splits the Schwarzschild chart into two disconnected pieces, with t and r exchanging roles inside.
Tool 3: spatial and spacetime diagrams of light flashes, built in flat space first, as the way to read causal structure.
Model: integrate radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild coordinates and draw the resulting light cones, which appear to show that nothing reaches r = 2m in finite time.
Check with a massive particle: proper time to reach r = 0 is finite (and Newtonian), whereas coordinate time diverges, so the Schwarzschild chart is the culprit.
Repair: define a new time that straightens ingoing null rays (advanced Eddington-Finkelstein), obtain a metric regular across r = 2m, and justify the analytic extension by patches and isometries.
Interpret: light cones tilt continuously, r = 2m is a one-way null surface, hence an absolute event horizon; the time-reversed (retarded) construction gives a white hole.
Application: spherical collapse of a star, signals to a distant observer, fading due to infinite redshift.
Bridge and intuition: Newtonian escape velocity gives the same critical radius; Newtonian and relativistic tidal stretching become unbounded at r = 0.
Reality check: observational evidence and the theoretical status of black holes, ending with Penrose's point that horizons need not involve high density.
signature_moves: Deliberately scrambling the coordinate labels (theta as x'^0, t as x'^2) to shock the reader out of reading meaning into symbols.
Using the sign of a single inverse-metric component as a one-line test for the character of each coordinate.
Building the curved-space diagrams by first drawing the same constructions in Minkowski space (point flashes, stacked snapshots, cones).
Presenting a diagram that is explicitly flagged as misleading (Fig. 17.7), then letting a proper-time calculation expose why.
Placing proper time and coordinate time for the same infall on one plot (Fig. 17.8).
Designing a coordinate transformation by demanding that a chosen family of light rays become straight 45 degree lines.
Arguing the legitimacy of an extension from the two metrics and their overlap rather than from the singular transformation itself, with an analytic-continuation analogy.
Pairing every black-hole construction with its time reverse (retarded coordinates, white hole, white-hole collapse exercise).
Closing a highly mathematical chapter with a list of honest objections and their current status.

sections.title: Characterization of coordinates
sections.summary: Raises the question of what coordinates mean when any transformation is allowed, illustrated by relabelling Schwarzschild's coordinates so that theta sits in the zeroth slot. Offers a coordinate-independent test: the gradient of a coordinate is the normal to its level surface, and its squared length equals the diagonal inverse-metric component g^(a)(a), whose sign fixes the character. Notes that coordinates may be any mixture of timelike, null and spacelike (common cases 1+3, 1 null + 3, 2 null + 2) as long as the normals are independent, and that symmetries single out adapted coordinates when Killing vectors commute. Applies this to (15.52): for r > 2m, t is timelike and the static world time, r is the areal radius, and theta, phi are the symmetry-defined angles, so Schwarzschild coordinates are canonical.

sections.title: Singularities
sections.summary: Explains that a chart generally covers only part of a manifold. The polar axis is a coordinate singularity cured by Cartesian coordinates. The metric also degenerates at r = 2m (the Schwarzschild radius) and r = 0; the Kretschmann scalar 48 m^2 r^-6 is finite at the former and infinite at the latter, suggesting r = 2m is removable and r = 0 is a genuine curvature singularity. Since g_00 vanishes at r = 2m, it is also a surface of infinite redshift. Contrasts the usual reading (exterior field of a body of radius a > 2m, with an interior solution inside) with the programme of studying the vacuum metric for all r, where r = 2m is null and separates region I (r > 2m) from region II (0 < r < 2m), in which t becomes spacelike and r timelike.

sections.title: Spatial and space-time diagrams
sections.summary: Introduces the diagnostic of local light-cone structure: the future light cone at a point is the set of null directions, light rays are tangent to it, and observers' world lines must stay inside it. Two kinds of picture are defined in Minkowski space: spatial diagrams showing where flashes emitted from many points at one time have spread by a later time (spheres, or circles with one dimension suppressed), and spacetime diagrams that stack successive snapshots of a single flash vertically in time, producing a cone (or a V with two dimensions suppressed); the past cone is added as a light front closing in on the event. Curvature will show up as cones that are narrowed, widened or tilted.

sections.title: Space-time diagram in Schwarzschild coordinates
sections.summary: Finds radial null geodesics from the Lagrangian 2K = 0 with dtheta = dphi = 0. The t equation gives a conserved (1 - 2m/r) t-dot = k, so r-dot = +/- k and r is itself an affine parameter. Writing dt/dr = r/(r - 2m) and integrating yields outgoing rays t = r + 2m ln|r - 2m| + const and ingoing rays with the opposite sign; t -> -t swaps them. The resulting diagram (Fig. 17.7), in which each point is a 2-sphere of area 4 pi r^2, shows 45 degree cones at large r, cones that close up near r = 2m, and cones tipped over in region II so that observers there must move to r = 0. The diagram appears to say that neither particles nor light reach r = 2m in finite time, but the authors warn that this is misleading because I and II are separate charts.

sections.title: A radially infalling particle
sections.summary: For a timelike radial geodesic (2K = 1) with energy constant k = 1 (released from rest at infinity), (dtau/dr)^2 = r/2m. Taking the root appropriate to infall and integrating gives a proper time that is finite all the way to r = 0 and coincides with the Newtonian free-fall formula. Using t instead, dt/dr contains a factor (1 - 2m/r)^-1, the integral has a logarithm that diverges at r = 2m, and near the horizon r - 2m shrinks like exp(-(t - t0)/2m). Fig. 17.8 contrasts the two descriptions. Because t is the proper time of distant static observers it is physically meaningful far away, but it is the wrong clock for infall and the chart itself fails at r = 2m.

sections.title: Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
sections.summary: Designs a new time t-bar = t + 2m ln(r - 2m) so that ingoing radial light rays become straight lines t-bar = -r + const. Substituting gives the Eddington-Finkelstein line element (17.22), which is regular and invertible at r = 2m and on the whole range 0 < r < infinity, so the manifold can be enlarged (an analytic extension, Fig. 17.9). The authors answer the objection that the transformation is singular at r = 2m: the real objects are two metrics, each regular on its largest domain, related by an isometry on the overlap r > 2m; inside, a different transformation with ln(2m - r) maps onto region II. The extension is not time symmetric; t* = t - 2m ln(r - 2m) straightens outgoing rays and gives a different extension. The null coordinate v = t-bar + r (advanced time) simplifies the metric to (17.24), with ingoing rays v = const. In Fig. 17.10 one edge of every cone stays at -45 degrees, the other rotates from +45 degrees at infinity to vertical at r = 2m and inward below it, and a radially infalling particle now crosses r = 2m smoothly.

sections.title: Event horizons
sections.summary: Restores angular information with an equatorial spatial diagram (Fig. 17.11): far away, flash fronts are centred circles as in flat space; closer in they are displaced inward; at r = 2m only the radially outward photon holds its position; inside, every front moves toward the singularity. Hence r = 2m is a one-way membrane that future-directed causal curves can cross only inward, and it bounds the events any outside observer could ever see: an event horizon. Unlike the observer-dependent horizons of hyperbolic motion (§3.8), it is absolute. Using the retarded null coordinate w = t* - r gives (17.26), again regular for all r > 0 but describing the time reverse (Fig. 17.12), a white hole whose horizon admits only past-directed curves inward.

sections.title: Black holes
sections.summary: Motivates collapse from stellar evolution: above the white dwarf and neutron star limits no pressure can halt contraction, and spherical collapse ends with all matter at the central singularity. Gives scale (Schwarzschild radius about 1 cm for Earth, 3 km for the Sun) and uses Birkhoff-type reasoning (the exterior of a spherical star stays Schwarzschild) to draw collapse on an Eddington-Finkelstein diagram (Fig. 17.13). A comoving observer passes r = 2m, but regularly spaced signals reach a distant observer at ever longer intervals, the signal sent at r = 2m never leaves, and later ones fall to the singularity. The distant observer in principle only sees the star just before it crossed, but infinite redshift makes it fade quickly, leaving a black hole. A three-dimensional version (Fig. 17.14) shows the collapsing star, the horizon cylinder and the singularity.

sections.title: A Newtonian argument
sections.summary: Shows that a restricted notion of a black hole (light unable to reach distant regions) already follows from Newtonian gravity if light is treated as particles. Energy conservation gives the escape speed v_0^2 = 2GM/R; setting v_0 = c defines a critical radius R = 2GM/c^2, which is exactly 2m in relativistic units. Laplace noted in 1798 that a body with the Sun's density and 250 times its radius would trap light.

sections.title: Tidal forces in a black hole
sections.summary: Recalls that a freely falling Newtonian dust sphere becomes a prolate ellipsoid of equal volume, stretched along the fall and squeezed across it. In general relativity the geodesic deviation equation, projected onto the orthonormal frame (17.32)-(17.35) built from Schwarzschild coordinates, gives radial relative acceleration +2m/r^3 times separation and transverse -m/r^3 times separation, so stretching and compression grow without bound as r -> 0. An astronaut falling feet first is pulled apart lengthwise and crushed sideways, ultimately at the atomic level.

sections.title: Observational evidence for black holes
sections.summary: Surveys indirect and direct evidence. X-ray binaries: the orbit of a visible star gives the mass of an unseen compact partner; if it exceeds neutron-star limits it is a black-hole candidate, and accreted gas heats and emits X-rays (Fig. 17.18). Cygnus X-1 (rapid X-ray variability found by Uhuru, 1971) has a supergiant companion and a compact mass above nine solar masses, versus limits of roughly 1.4 and 4 solar masses for white dwarfs and neutron stars. LIGO's September 2015 signal matched the merger of black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses. Active galactic nuclei are modelled with supermassive black holes; stellar proper motions at the Milky Way centre imply about 2.6 million solar masses in a small region. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the M87 source (data 2017, image 2019) in agreement with lensing predictions.

sections.title: Theoretical status of black holes
sections.summary: Lists objections and responses. Too symmetric: charged and rotating solutions keep horizons and singularities (the text points to Chapters 18 and 19, but in this edition these are Chapters 19 and 20). Asymmetries excluded: perturbation studies suggest asymmetries are radiated away and the hole settles to Schwarzschild (Fig. 17.19). Wrong field equations: the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems need only a metric theory, causality and energy conditions, and show collapse produces inextendible geodesics, though not where or what the singularity is. Unsolved: no realistic interior matched to Kerr, so stability might fail; quantum gravity might halt collapse with a bounce. Finally, Penrose's scaling: mean density goes as 1/m^2, so supermassive holes have low density and gentle horizon tides, meaning horizons do not require extreme physics.
concepts: no-hair relaxation of perturbed black holes

concepts.name: arbitrariness of coordinate labels
concepts.definition: Because a metric solving the field equations remains a solution under any smooth change of coordinates, the labels x^a have no built-in physical or geometrical meaning; significance must be established from invariant properties such as causal character, symmetries or curvature scalars.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as a puzzle: apply a wild transformation to Schwarzschild and ask someone to interpret it. A trivial reshuffle (theta placed in the time slot) shows you cannot assume the zeroth coordinate is a time.
concepts.notes: Exercise 17.1 presents Schwarzschild with the labels scrambled and asks for an interpretation.

concepts.name: causal character of a coordinate
concepts.definition: For a coordinate x^(a), the gradient n_b = partial_b x^(a) is normal to the level surfaces x^(a) = const and has squared norm g^(a)(a). With signature (+,-,-,-) the coordinate is called timelike, null or spacelike when g^(a)(a) is positive, zero or negative; in standard terminology a positive value means the level surface itself is spacelike (it has a timelike normal).
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the one invariant thing that can be said about an arbitrary coordinate; the computation takes three lines and is then applied to Schwarzschild's inverse metric (17.2).
concepts.notes: The book attaches the words timelike/spacelike to the hypersurface where standard usage would call the hypersurface spacelike/timelike; see gaps_and_pitfalls. The mixtures met most often are one time coordinate with three spatial ones, one null coordinate with three spatial ones (as in Eddington-Finkelstein v, r, theta, phi), and a pair of null coordinates with two spatial ones (as in Kruskal-type charts). The only requirement is that the four gradient normals are linearly independent.

concepts.name: normal covector to a hypersurface
concepts.definition: For a hypersurface given as f(x) = const, the covector n_b = partial_b f is orthogonal to every vector tangent to the surface; raising the index with g^{ab} gives the normal vector, whose norm determines the causal type of the surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the computational route to classifying coordinates: for f = x^(a) the gradient is a Kronecker delta.

concepts.name: Killing-adapted coordinates
concepts.definition: If a spacetime has a Killing vector field one can choose coordinates in which it equals partial/partial x^a for one coordinate, so the metric components do not depend on that coordinate; several Killing fields can be adapted simultaneously exactly when they commute (vanishing Lie brackets).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 15 as the reason symmetric solutions possess preferred coordinates, then used to certify t, theta, phi in Schwarzschild.
concepts.notes: Non-commuting symmetries (e.g. the rotation group) still constrain coordinates but less directly. Exercise 17.4 applies the idea to Dingle's metric.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild coordinates
concepts.definition: The coordinates (t, r, theta, phi) in which the Schwarzschild metric takes the form (15.52): t is the static Killing time, r is the areal radius, and theta, phi are standard angles on the symmetry spheres. They are regular only for r > 2m (region I) or separately for 0 < r < 2m (region II), away from the polar axis.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified in §17.1 as invariantly defined by the symmetries, then shown in §§17.4-17.5 to be unsuitable for describing infall through r = 2m.

concepts.name: areal radius
concepts.definition: A radial coordinate defined so that the symmetry 2-sphere labelled r has proper area 4 pi r^2 (equivalently circumference 2 pi r); it is not the proper radial distance from the centre.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the induced line element on t = const, r = const, and contrasted with the isotropic radius rho of (15.63), which lacks this property.

concepts.name: static spacetime and world time
concepts.definition: A spacetime is static when it has a hypersurface-orthogonal timelike Killing vector; in adapted coordinates the metric is independent of t and has no dt dx^alpha cross terms, and t is an invariantly defined time (world time) up to scale and origin.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from §15.3 to identify Schwarzschild t, valid only where the Killing vector is timelike (r > 2m).
concepts.notes: Inside r = 2m the same Killing vector is spacelike, so the region II metric is not static.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A place where a metric's components in a given chart become degenerate or infinite only because the coordinates fail there; a different chart covers the points smoothly and all curvature invariants stay finite.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with the familiar polar axis theta = 0, pi, cured by Cartesian coordinates, then applied to r = 2m.
concepts.notes: Finite invariants are evidence, not proof, of removability; the proof is the explicit regular chart (17.22).

concepts.name: curvature singularity
concepts.definition: A singularity that no change of coordinates can remove, signalled for example by a curvature scalar diverging along curves that reach it in finite affine parameter; at r = 0 in Schwarzschild tidal forces become unbounded.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified at r = 0 by the divergence of the Kretschmann scalar, listed with its many synonyms, and later given physical meaning through infinite tides (§17.10) and the singularity theorems (§17.12).

concepts.name: Kretschmann scalar
concepts.definition: The full contraction R_{abcd} R^{abcd} of the Riemann tensor with itself; being a scalar it has the same value in every chart, and for Schwarzschild it equals 48 m^2/r^6.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without derivation as the invariant test that separates r = 2m (finite) from r = 0 (divergent).
concepts.notes: Ricci scalar and Ricci tensor vanish in vacuum, so a quadratic Riemann invariant is the simplest non-trivial test.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.definition: The areal radius r_s = 2GM/c^2 (2m in geometric units) at which the Schwarzschild metric component g_00 vanishes; it locates the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in §17.2 as a place where the metric degenerates, given numerical scale in §17.8 (Earth about 1 cm, Sun 3 km), and recovered by a Newtonian escape-speed argument in §17.9.

concepts.name: surface of infinite redshift
concepts.definition: A surface on which the timelike Killing vector becomes null (g_00 = 0 in static coordinates), so light emitted by a static source there would reach infinity with infinite redshift; in Schwarzschild it coincides with r = 2m.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted in one sentence from the redshift formula (16.4), and cashed in §17.8 to explain why a collapsing star fades from view.
concepts.notes: For Kerr the infinite-redshift surface and horizon separate (ergosphere); here they coincide.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild vacuum solution
concepts.definition: The unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equations, with line element (15.52); physically it describes the field outside any spherical mass distribution, and taken on its own for all r it describes an eternal non-rotating black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 15; the standard reading as an exterior field (Fig. 17.1) is contrasted with the programme of studying the metric for every r without a source.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild interior solution
concepts.definition: Schwarzschild's static, spherically symmetric perfect-fluid solution of uniform density, which can be matched to the vacuum exterior at the surface r = a.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the standard example of the non-vacuum metric that would replace the exterior inside a real star.

concepts.name: regions I and II of Schwarzschild
concepts.definition: The two disconnected coordinate domains of the Schwarzschild chart: region I with 2m < r < infinity, where t is timelike, and region II with 0 < r < 2m, where r is timelike; in Schwarzschild coordinates they cannot be joined, but Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates show they are pieces of one connected spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced after dropping the stellar source: the null surface r = 2m separates the chart into two parts, which the authors insist must initially be treated as separate spacetimes.

concepts.name: interchange of t and r inside the horizon
aliases: t spacelike and r timelike for r < 2m
concepts.definition: For 0 < r < 2m the signs of g_00 and g_11 in Schwarzschild coordinates reverse, so t labels a spatial direction and r becomes a time coordinate; decreasing r is then as unavoidable as the passage of time.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the sign flips in the inverse metric (17.2) and illustrated by light cones that tip over in Fig. 17.7.
prerequisites: regions I and II of Schwarzschild

concepts.name: local light cone
concepts.definition: At a point P, the set of null directions (tangent vectors with g_ab k^a k^b = 0); its future half contains all possible directions of light rays leaving P, and every future-directed timelike world line through P points into its interior.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the main interpretive technique of the chapter, with light rays tangent to the cone and observers confined inside it.

concepts.name: null geodesic
concepts.definition: A geodesic whose tangent is everywhere null; in geometrical optics it is the path of a light ray.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken as known and used to define light cones and then the radial null congruences.

concepts.name: spatial light-flash diagram
concepts.definition: A picture of space at one moment showing, for flashes emitted from several points at an earlier time, where each wave front has reached; in flat space the fronts are spheres (or circles) centred on their emission points.
concepts.how_introduced: Built first for Minkowski space (Figs. 17.2-17.3) and later redrawn for Schwarzschild in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates (Fig. 17.11), where fronts are displaced toward the centre.

concepts.name: spacetime diagram with suppressed dimensions
concepts.definition: A plot with time vertical and one or two spatial dimensions shown, made by stacking spatial snapshots; a flash from P becomes a cone (one dimension suppressed) or a pair of 45 degree lines (two suppressed), and in spherical symmetry each point of a (t, r) diagram stands for a 2-sphere of area 4 pi r^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by stacking snapshots of an expanding flash (Figs. 17.4-17.6), then used for Schwarzschild, Eddington-Finkelstein and collapse diagrams.

concepts.name: radial null geodesics of Schwarzschild
concepts.definition: The light rays with theta, phi constant; in Schwarzschild coordinates they satisfy dt/dr = +/- r/(r - 2m), giving outgoing curves t = r + 2m ln|r - 2m| + const and ingoing curves t = -(r + 2m ln|r - 2m|) + const.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived with the variational method, checked by the t -> -t symmetry, and drawn as Fig. 17.7; later straightened by Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates.
prerequisites: conserved energy constant from time-translation symmetry
concepts.notes: The combination r + 2m ln|r/2m - 1| is the tortoise coordinate in other texts; D'Inverno does not name it.

concepts.name: variational method for geodesics
concepts.definition: Geodesics extremize the integral of K = (1/2) g_ab x-dot^a x-dot^b with respect to an affine parameter; the Euler-Lagrange equations give the geodesic equations, with the first integral 2K = 0 for null and 2K = 1 for timelike curves parametrized by proper time (in +--- signature).
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked by reference to (7.47) to shortcut the geodesic equations for radial null and timelike motion.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic in which the geodesic equation takes its standard form (tangent parallel-transported with no rescaling term); affine parameters are unique up to u -> a u + b.
concepts.how_introduced: Arises when r-dot = +/- k shows r is a linear function of the affine parameter on radial null geodesics.

concepts.name: conserved energy constant from time-translation symmetry
concepts.definition: Because the Schwarzschild metric does not depend on t, the momentum conjugate to t, k = (1 - 2m/r) dt/du, is constant along any geodesic; for timelike geodesics k is the energy per unit rest mass measured at infinity, with k = 1 for release from rest at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the first integral of the t Euler-Lagrange equation for null rays (17.5) and for massive infall (17.12).

concepts.name: light-cone tipping inside the horizon
concepts.definition: In coordinates adapted to the geometry, the future light cones progressively tilt toward smaller r as r decreases; at r = 2m the outward edge is vertical so an outgoing radial photon stays at fixed r, and inside every future direction points to smaller r.
concepts.how_introduced: Seen first in the Schwarzschild-coordinate diagram (Fig. 17.7), where cones collapse at r = 2m and reappear sideways in II, then shown continuously in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates (Fig. 17.10).

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The property that the metric approaches the Minkowski metric at large distances from the source, so light cones become 45 degree cones in suitable units.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain why Schwarzschild null curves make 45 degree angles as r -> infinity.

concepts.name: radial free fall in Schwarzschild
concepts.definition: A timelike radial geodesic; for release from rest at infinity (k = 1) the proper time satisfies (dtau/dr)^2 = r/2m, so the particle travels from r_0 to r = 0 in finite proper time given by the Newtonian formula, passing r = 2m without incident.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked out in §17.5 as a check on the suspicious Schwarzschild-coordinate diagram; later drawn as a smooth dashed curve in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates.
prerequisites: conserved energy constant from time-translation symmetry

concepts.name: proper time versus coordinate time
concepts.definition: Proper time is what a clock carried along a world line records and is invariant; a coordinate time is merely a label and may run to infinity along a world line that ends in finite proper time. Schwarzschild t equals the proper time of static observers at infinity, not of infallers.
concepts.how_introduced: Dramatized by Fig. 17.8, where the same infall is plotted against tau (reaching r = 0) and against t (asymptotic to r = 2m).

concepts.name: exponential approach to the horizon in coordinate time
concepts.definition: As described by Schwarzschild time, an infalling body near r = 2m obeys r - 2m approximately proportional to exp(-t/2m), so it approaches but never reaches the horizon as t -> infinity; in physical units the e-folding time is 2GM/c^3.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by keeping the dominant 1/(r - 2m) term in dt/dr (Exercise 17.12), then explained as a coordinate artefact.
concepts.notes: The 2m e-folding refers to Schwarzschild t along the infaller's world line. What a distant observer receives is labelled by retarded time, in which the approach (and the redshift of received light) e-folds over 4m.

concepts.name: Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates obtained from Schwarzschild by t-bar = t + 2m ln(r - 2m) (or equivalently the null coordinate v = t-bar + r), chosen so ingoing radial light rays are straight; the resulting metric is regular and invertible for all 0 < r < infinity and covers regions I and II smoothly.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the failure of t for infall; derived by demanding straight ingoing null rays, used to extend the solution and to draw correct light-cone and collapse diagrams.
concepts.notes: Retarded (outgoing) versions use t* = t - 2m ln(r - 2m) and w = t* - r.

concepts.name: advanced time
concepts.definition: The null coordinate v = t-bar + r (equivalently t + r + 2m ln(r - 2m)) whose level surfaces are ingoing radial null hypersurfaces; in (v, r, theta, phi) the Schwarzschild metric reads (1 - 2m/r) dv^2 - 2 dv dr - r^2 dOmega^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to simplify (17.22); ingoing rays are then simply v = const.

concepts.name: retarded time
concepts.definition: The null coordinate w = t* - r with t* = t - 2m ln(r - 2m), constant on outgoing radial null hypersurfaces; in (w, r, theta, phi) the metric is (1 - 2m/r) dw^2 + 2 dw dr - r^2 dOmega^2, regular for r > 0 and describing the time-reversed (white hole) extension.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced after the event-horizon discussion as the time reverse of the advanced construction.
prerequisites: time asymmetry of the Eddington-Finkelstein extension

concepts.name: analytic extension
concepts.definition: Enlarging a spacetime by finding a metric on a bigger manifold that is isometric to the original on the original region and regular beyond it; here the Eddington-Finkelstein metric on 0 < r < infinity extends Schwarzschild region I.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by Fig. 17.9 (hatched region of good coordinates growing) and likened to analytic continuation in complex analysis; the legitimacy is argued via maximal regular domains and an isometry on the overlap.
concepts.notes: The extension is not unique: advanced and retarded coordinates give different extensions, resolved in the maximal Kruskal extension (Chapter 18).

concepts.name: isometry between coordinate patches
concepts.definition: A diffeomorphism between (parts of) two spacetimes that carries one metric into the other; isometric regions are the same geometry described in different coordinates.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to say the r > 2m part of (17.22) is region I of (15.52) via (17.19), and the r < 2m part is region II via a separate map with ln(2m - r).

concepts.name: time asymmetry of the Eddington-Finkelstein extension
concepts.definition: Although Schwarzschild is invariant under t -> -t, each Eddington-Finkelstein extension is not: straightening ingoing rays produces a region II into which things can fall (black hole), while straightening outgoing rays produces a different region II out of which things can emerge (white hole).
concepts.how_introduced: Noted right after the extension argument and developed in §17.7 with the retarded coordinate.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: The boundary of the set of events from which future-directed causal curves can reach distant external observers; for Schwarzschild it is the null surface r = 2m, which future-directed timelike and null curves can cross only inward and which hides region II from every outside observer.
concepts.how_introduced: Inferred from the Eddington-Finkelstein light cones and the spatial diagram of dragged wave fronts, called a one-way membrane, and contrasted with the horizons of accelerated observers.

concepts.name: one-way membrane
concepts.definition: A null hypersurface that future-directed causal curves can cross in one direction only; for the black-hole extension the direction is inward, and for the white-hole extension the roles are reversed (only past-directed curves cross inward).
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the direct visual reading of Fig. 17.11 and then applied again to the retarded solution.

concepts.name: observer-dependent horizon
concepts.definition: A horizon that exists only relative to a particular family of observers, e.g. the boundary of events a uniformly accelerating observer can ever receive signals from; a different (inertial) observer has no such horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from §3.8 to sharpen, by contrast, why the Schwarzschild horizon is absolute.

concepts.name: white hole
concepts.definition: The time reverse of a black hole: a region from which future-directed causal curves can only exit and which nothing can enter from outside in the future; for Schwarzschild it arises from the retarded Eddington-Finkelstein extension.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when the retarded line element (17.26) is shown to describe the time reversal of (17.22); Exercise 17.17 asks for the white-hole analogue of collapse.
prerequisites: time asymmetry of the Eddington-Finkelstein extension

concepts.name: black hole
concepts.definition: A region of spacetime from which no causal curve can escape to distant regions, bounded by an event horizon; the non-rotating uncharged case is described by the advanced Eddington-Finkelstein extension of Schwarzschild and contains a curvature singularity at r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Built up in stages: extension through r = 2m, one-way horizon, then physical formation by collapse, with the name introduced for the dark remnant left as a star fades.

concepts.name: gravitational collapse
concepts.definition: The unhalted contraction of a star whose self-gravity exceeds the support of pressure and stresses; in spherical symmetry the exterior stays Schwarzschild, the surface crosses r = 2m in finite proper time, and all matter reaches the central singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated from stellar evolution and drawn on Eddington-Finkelstein diagrams in 2D (Fig. 17.13) and 3D (Fig. 17.14).
prerequisites: maximum mass of white dwarfs and neutron stars
concepts.notes: That the exterior remains Schwarzschild is Birkhoff's theorem, used here without being named.

concepts.name: maximum mass of white dwarfs and neutron stars
concepts.definition: The largest mass that electron degeneracy (white dwarfs, about 1.4 solar masses) or neutron degeneracy plus nuclear forces (neutron stars, a few solar masses) can support; a compact remnant heavier than this cannot be in equilibrium.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to motivate collapse in §17.8 and to classify Cygnus X-1's compact companion in §17.11.
concepts.notes: The book's neutron-star value of about 4 solar masses is a generous upper bound; current estimates are closer to 2.2-2.5 solar masses.

concepts.name: Newtonian escape velocity
concepts.definition: The minimum launch speed from the surface of a spherical mass M of radius R that lets a projectile reach infinity with zero speed: v_0 = sqrt(2GM/R), from setting the total Newtonian energy to zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in §17.9 as the route to a Newtonian analogue of the black hole (Fig. 17.15).

concepts.name: Newtonian dark star
concepts.definition: A Newtonian body so compact that the escape speed at its surface exceeds c, so corpuscular light cannot reach infinity; the critical radius 2GM/c^2 coincides numerically with the Schwarzschild radius.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a restricted, pre-relativistic version of the black-hole idea, credited to Laplace.
concepts.notes: Physically different from a relativistic horizon: Newtonian light could climb some distance and fall back, and a slower-than-escape projectile could be observed from nearby; the agreement of the radius is partly a coincidence.

concepts.name: geodesic deviation
concepts.definition: The relative acceleration of neighbouring freely falling particles is governed by curvature: in a frame parallel-transported along one geodesic, D^2 eta^alpha / D tau^2 = - R^alpha_{0 beta 0} eta^beta for the spatial connecting vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from (10.38)-(10.39) and evaluated in Schwarzschild as the relativistic measure of tides.

concepts.name: orthonormal static frame
concepts.definition: The frame obtained by normalizing the Schwarzschild coordinate basis vectors: e_0 along partial_t scaled by (1 - 2m/r)^(-1/2), e_1 along partial_r scaled by (1 - 2m/r)^(1/2), e_2 = r^-1 partial_theta, e_3 = (r sin theta)^-1 partial_phi; it is orthonormal only for r > 2m.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated with the 'holds in these coordinates' symbol and used to project the Riemann tensor for the tidal equations (orthonormality is Exercise 17.18).

concepts.name: tidal acceleration
concepts.definition: The difference in gravitational acceleration across an extended body; for a body falling radially toward a mass m at radius r, the radial separation grows at rate 2m/r^3 (stretching) while transverse separations shrink at rate m/r^3 (compression), with volume preserved to first order.
concepts.how_introduced: First in Newtonian form with a dust sphere becoming an ellipsoid (Fig. 17.16), then from geodesic deviation in Schwarzschild (17.37)-(17.39).

concepts.name: spaghettification
aliases: tidal disruption of an infalling observer
concepts.definition: The stretching of an infalling body along the radial direction and squeezing across it by tidal forces that grow without bound near r = 0, ultimately disrupting any material object.
concepts.how_introduced: Narrated as an astronaut falling feet first (Fig. 17.17); the book does not use the popular name.

concepts.name: X-ray binary
concepts.definition: A binary system with an ordinary star and a compact companion that pulls gas from it; the gas forms a hot accretion disc emitting X-rays, and the companion's mass inferred from the visible star's orbit can rule out a neutron star.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the first class of black-hole evidence, with Cygnus X-1 and the schematic Fig. 17.18.
prerequisites: maximum mass of white dwarfs and neutron stars

concepts.name: accretion disc
concepts.definition: A rotating disc of gas spiralling onto a compact object, heated by viscous dissipation so that its inner parts radiate strongly (X-rays for stellar-mass black holes).
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the source of X-ray emission in binaries and as the target imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope.
concepts.notes: The book attributes the X-rays to synchrotron radiation; thermal and Comptonized emission dominate in most models.

concepts.name: binary black hole merger
aliases: gravitational waves from merging black holes
concepts.definition: The inspiral and coalescence of two black holes, which emits gravitational waves whose waveform can be compared with general-relativistic predictions to infer the component masses.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as more direct evidence via LIGO's 2015 detection, with details deferred to Chapter 21.

concepts.name: supermassive black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole of millions to billions of solar masses at the centre of a galaxy, invoked to power active galactic nuclei and inferred in the Milky Way from stellar orbits.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced through active galaxies and the Milky Way's central mass; used again in §17.12 for the low-density, weak-tide argument.

concepts.name: horizon-scale imaging
concepts.definition: Very-long-baseline interferometry with Earth-sized baselines resolving emission near a supermassive black hole, so the strongly lensed image (a bright ring around a dark shadow) can be compared with general relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Described briefly as further direct evidence, with the 2017 observation and 2019 image of the M87 source.
concepts.notes: The book calls the EHT an optical array; it is a millimetre-wavelength radio interferometer.

concepts.name: no-hair relaxation of perturbed black holes
concepts.definition: Perturbation studies indicate that deviations from symmetry in collapse are shed as gravitational radiation, so a non-rotating uncharged collapse settles asymptotically into a Schwarzschild black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to answer the objection that exact spherical symmetry forces the singular outcome (Fig. 17.19).

concepts.name: singularity theorems
concepts.definition: Results showing that under general assumptions (a metric theory of gravity, reasonable causality, energy conditions and suitable initial trapping or expansion conditions) spacetime contains incomplete causal geodesics; they establish that something singular occurs without locating or characterizing the singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to answer the objection that singular collapse is an artefact of GR's specific field equations or of symmetry; details deferred to §20.13.

concepts.name: energy conditions
concepts.definition: Inequalities on the energy-momentum tensor (for example positivity of energy density measured by any observer) that express physically reasonable matter and are inputs to the singularity theorems.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among the mild assumptions of the singularity theorems, with a caution that strong fields might violate them.

concepts.name: geodesic incompleteness
concepts.definition: A geodesic is incomplete if it cannot be extended to arbitrarily large affine parameter; incomplete timelike or null geodesics are the standard definition of a singular spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as what the singularity theorems actually prove, with the usual interpretation that such geodesics end at a singularity.

concepts.name: interior matching problem
concepts.definition: The unsolved task of finding a realistic matter solution inside a rotating body that joins smoothly to the exterior Kerr metric; without it, the stability of collapse cannot be analysed in detail.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as an unresolved difficulty in the theoretical status of black holes.

concepts.name: quantum gravity bounce
concepts.definition: The proposal, in some quantum gravity approaches, that quantum effects halt collapse before a singularity forms and produce a rebound.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as a possible modification of the classical endpoint at high density.

concepts.name: black hole mean density scaling
concepts.definition: Since the horizon radius is proportional to the mass and the enclosed coordinate volume to the radius cubed, the mean density (mass over 4 pi r_s^3 / 3) scales as 1/M^2, so sufficiently massive black holes form at low density; the horizon tidal acceleration likewise falls as 1/M^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Credited to Penrose to rebut the idea that black holes require exotic high-density physics.
concepts.notes: The 'volume' is the Euclidean 4 pi r_s^3/3, a heuristic rather than a proper spatial volume.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild line element (recalled)
key_equations.meaning: The metric under study throughout the chapter, written in canonical Schwarzschild coordinates; degenerate at r = 2m, r = 0 and on the polar axis.
key_equations.symbols: m = GM/c^2 geometric mass; t static time; r areal radius

key_equations.name: coordinate hypersurface
key_equations.meaning: Level surface of one fixed coordinate, whose causal character is to be tested.
key_equations.symbols: parentheses: index held fixed, no summation

key_equations.name: normal covector and vector
key_equations.meaning: The gradient of a coordinate is normal to its level surface; raising the index picks out a column of the inverse metric.

key_equations.name: norm of the normal
key_equations.meaning: The squared length of the normal equals the diagonal inverse-metric component, so its sign decides whether the coordinate is timelike (>0), null (=0) or spacelike (<0) in the book's usage.

key_equations.name: inverse Schwarzschild metric
key_equations.meaning: Diagonal inverse components: for r > 2m, t is timelike and r, theta, phi spacelike; for r < 2m the first two signs flip so t and r swap character; g^11 = 0 at r = 2m marks a null surface.

key_equations.name: metric on symmetry spheres
key_equations.meaning: Induced line element on t, r constant, showing the sphere has area 4 pi r^2 and so r is the areal radius.

key_equations.name: Cartesian coordinates near the axis
key_equations.meaning: Change of chart that removes the polar-axis coordinate singularity.

key_equations.name: Kretschmann scalar of Schwarzschild
key_equations.meaning: Chart-independent curvature measure: finite at r = 2m (removable singularity) and divergent at r = 0 (curvature singularity).

key_equations.name: null condition
key_equations.meaning: Light rays are null curves tangent to the local light cone.

key_equations.name: radial null condition
key_equations.meaning: Restricts to light rays moving purely radially.
key_equations.symbols: dot: derivative with respect to affine parameter u

key_equations.name: null Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: First integral of the geodesic equations for radial light rays.

key_equations.name: t Euler-Lagrange equation
key_equations.meaning: Since the metric does not depend on t, its conjugate momentum is conserved.

key_equations.name: energy constant (null)
key_equations.meaning: Conserved quantity from time-translation symmetry along a null geodesic.
Substituting the energy constant into the null condition removes the metric factors.
Radial coordinate changes linearly with affine parameter, so r is itself affine on radial null geodesics; signs give outgoing and ingoing rays.
Chain rule to get the ray shape t(r) without solving parametrically.

key_equations.name: slope of outgoing radial null rays
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate slope of outgoing rays; tends to 1 at large r, diverges at r = 2m and is negative for 0 < r < 2m.

key_equations.name: outgoing radial null geodesics
key_equations.meaning: Outgoing light rays in Schwarzschild coordinates; the logarithm makes them asymptote to r = 2m as t -> -infinity.

key_equations.name: outgoing criterion
key_equations.meaning: In region I, r grows with t along (17.10), justifying the name outgoing.

key_equations.name: ingoing radial null geodesics
key_equations.meaning: Ingoing light rays; they approach r = 2m only as t -> +infinity in this chart. t -> -t exchanges (17.10) and (17.11).

key_equations.name: energy constant (timelike)
key_equations.meaning: Conserved energy per unit mass for radial free fall; k = 1 means released from rest at infinity.
key_equations.symbols: dot: derivative with respect to proper time tau

key_equations.name: timelike normalization
key_equations.meaning: Proper-time parametrization of a radial timelike geodesic (2K = 1).
With k = 1 the metric factors cancel, leaving a simple Newtonian-looking relation; the negative root is taken because r decreases during infall.

key_equations.name: proper time of radial infall
key_equations.meaning: Finite proper time to reach any r including 2m and 0; identical in form to Newtonian free fall from rest at infinity.
key_equations.symbols: r_0: radius at proper time tau_0

key_equations.name: coordinate-time slope for infall
key_equations.meaning: The factor (1 - 2m/r)^-1 makes t diverge as r -> 2m.

key_equations.name: coordinate time of radial infall
key_equations.meaning: Explicit Schwarzschild-time integral; agrees with (17.15) when r and r_0 are much larger than 2m, but the logarithm diverges as r -> 2m.

key_equations.name: near-horizon approach in coordinate time
key_equations.meaning: Close to the horizon the gap to r = 2m decays exponentially in t, never reaching zero for finite t: the frozen-star appearance.

key_equations.name: advanced Eddington-Finkelstein time
key_equations.meaning: Transformation for r > 2m designed so ingoing radial null rays become straight lines.

key_equations.name: straight ingoing rays
key_equations.meaning: Ingoing radial light rays at -45 degrees in the new coordinates.
Differential of (17.19), substituted for dt in (15.52).

key_equations.name: Eddington-Finkelstein line element
key_equations.meaning: Schwarzschild geometry in coordinates regular and invertible for all 0 < r < infinity (determinant -r^4 sin^2 theta), allowing extension through r = 2m.

key_equations.name: map for the inner region
key_equations.meaning: The transformation that shows the r < 2m part of (17.22) is isometric to Schwarzschild region II.

key_equations.name: retarded Eddington-Finkelstein time
key_equations.meaning: Alternative time that straightens outgoing radial null rays, yielding the time-reversed extension.

key_equations.name: advanced time
key_equations.meaning: Null coordinate constant along ingoing radial light rays.

key_equations.name: advanced null form of Schwarzschild
key_equations.meaning: Compact ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein metric; radial null rays are v = const (ingoing) and dv/dr = 2/(1 - 2m/r) (outgoing in region I, turning inward inside r = 2m).

key_equations.name: retarded time
key_equations.meaning: Null coordinate constant along outgoing radial light rays.

key_equations.name: retarded null form (white hole extension)
key_equations.meaning: Regular for 0 < r < infinity; the time reverse of (17.24), describing a white hole whose horizon only past-directed curves cross inward.

key_equations.name: Newtonian energy
key_equations.meaning: Conserved energy of a projectile moving radially outside a spherical mass.
key_equations.symbols: M: source mass; m: test mass

key_equations.name: escape velocity
key_equations.meaning: Speed at the surface needed to reach infinity with zero speed (E = 0).

key_equations.name: light-trapping condition
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian corpuscular light just escapes when the escape speed equals c.

key_equations.name: Newtonian critical radius
key_equations.meaning: The critical radius equals the Schwarzschild radius 2m in relativistic units.

key_equations.name: geodesic deviation in a frame
key_equations.meaning: Relative acceleration of neighbouring free particles determined by frame components of the Riemann tensor.
key_equations.symbols: eta^alpha: spatial connecting vector; e_i^a: orthonormal frame (e^alpha_a the dual)

key_equations.name: static frame, time leg
key_equations.meaning: Unit vector along the static Killing direction; defined only for r > 2m.

key_equations.name: static frame, radial leg
key_equations.meaning: Unit radial vector.

key_equations.name: static frame, theta leg
key_equations.meaning: Unit polar-angle vector.

key_equations.name: static frame, phi leg
key_equations.meaning: Unit azimuthal vector.
Labels frame components of the separation vector by the corresponding directions.

key_equations.name: radial tidal stretching
key_equations.meaning: Positive coefficient: radially separated particles accelerate apart (tension), unbounded as r -> 0.

key_equations.name: transverse tidal compression (theta)
key_equations.meaning: Negative coefficient: transversely separated particles are pushed together (pressure).

key_equations.name: transverse tidal compression (phi)
key_equations.meaning: Same compression in the second transverse direction; the three coefficients sum to zero, as required in vacuum.

key_equations.name: mean density scaling
key_equations.latex: R\propto m,\quad V\propto R^3\propto m^3\;\Rightarrow\;\bar\rho\propto m^{-2}
key_equations.meaning: Heuristic showing larger black holes have lower mean density inside the horizon.

figures.label: Fig. 17.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Usual reading of the Schwarzschild vacuum metric: it applies only outside a spherical body larger than its Schwarzschild radius.
figures.visual_description: Two concentric circles. The ring between the inner circle and the outer circle is hatched and represents the material body; a radius line from the centre is marked a (the body's surface radius). The inner circle, marked 2m and indicated by a leader labelled 'Schwarzschild radius', lies inside the body and is left unhatched as a reference. Outside the outer circle the words 'Schwarzschild' (above) and 'vacuum' (below) label the exterior region where the vacuum metric applies.
figures.what_it_teaches: The vacuum metric is normally only valid for r > a > 2m, with a different interior metric inside the body; the chapter will instead consider the vacuum metric at all r.

redesign.idea: Star-radius slider: a cross-section of a star with a shaded interior and the vacuum region outside, plus a dashed circle at 2m. As the learner shrinks the stellar radius a toward and past 2m, labels switch from 'interior metric here' to 'vacuum metric reaches r = 2m', introducing the question the chapter pursues.
redesign.interaction: Drag the stellar surface radius a; toggle between showing the areal-radius profile and g_00 along a radial line; a warning badge appears when a < 2m.

figures.label: Fig. 17.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Spatial picture of flat spacetime: flashes from several points spread as spheres centred on their sources.
figures.visual_description: Three-dimensional Cartesian axes x, y, z. Four small shaded spheres float at various positions, each with a dot at its centre marking where a flash was emitted.
figures.what_it_teaches: In Minkowski space every wave front is centred on its emission point and all fronts have the same size after the same time, a baseline for later curved-space diagrams.

redesign.idea: Flash field: the learner clicks anywhere in a 3D box to emit a flash; after a chosen delay the sphere of light around each click is drawn. Later the same tool can be switched to Schwarzschild (EF) mode where spheres shift inward, so flat and curved cases share one interface.
redesign.interaction: Click to place emitters, slider for elapsed time t2 - t1, orbit camera; mode switch flat/Schwarzschild.

figures.label: Fig. 17.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: The same flat-space spatial picture restricted to a plane, where the spheres become circles.
figures.visual_description: Two-dimensional axes x (horizontal) and y (vertical). Four circles sit at different positions, each with a central dot.
figures.what_it_teaches: Suppressing a spatial dimension keeps the essential information when there is symmetry; this is the template against which Fig. 17.11 is compared.

redesign.idea: Planar version of the flash-field tool, used as the flat reference panel shown side by side with the Schwarzschild equatorial panel (Fig. 17.11 redesign).
redesign.interaction: Click to add emitters; time slider; toggle 'show emission point' dots.

figures.label: Fig. 17.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: First of three snapshots of a single flash from P: at time t1 there is only the point.
figures.visual_description: 3D axes x, y, z with a single labelled dot P; label t1 under the axes.
figures.what_it_teaches: Starts the snapshot sequence whose stacking produces a light cone.

redesign.idea: Snapshot stacker: three (or a continuous range of) spatial frames of an expanding flash, which the learner can slide apart vertically; as frames separate the circles trace out a cone and the 'time axis' appears, turning a flip-book into a spacetime diagram.
redesign.interaction: Scrub time to grow the flash; drag a 'stack' slider that lifts each snapshot to height t; rotate the resulting 3D cone.

figures.label: Fig. 17.4 (second panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Second snapshot of the flash from P at a later time t2.
figures.visual_description: Same x, y, z axes; P at the centre of a small circle (the spreading front); label t2 > t1.
figures.what_it_teaches: The front has grown into a sphere (drawn as a circle) centred on P.

redesign.idea: Covered by the snapshot-stacker redesign of the first panel.
redesign.interaction: None separately; this panel is one frame of the animation.

figures.label: Fig. 17.4 (third panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Third snapshot of the flash at a still later time t3.
figures.visual_description: Same axes; a larger circle centred on P, labelled t3 > t2.
figures.what_it_teaches: The front keeps expanding at the speed of light, so its radius grows linearly with elapsed time.

redesign.idea: Covered by the snapshot-stacker redesign of the first panel.
redesign.interaction: None separately.

figures.label: Fig. 17.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Stacking the snapshots gives a spacetime diagram of the flash with one spatial dimension dropped.
figures.visual_description: Axes x, y horizontal (in perspective) and t vertical. From the event P at height t1 a cone opens upward; two ellipses on the cone mark the wave front at t2 and t3.
figures.what_it_teaches: The future light cone of P is the history of an expanding light front; ellipses represent circles in perspective.

redesign.idea: Same as the snapshot stacker: the finished cone, with an optional past cone as an imploding front and a draggable timelike world line that must stay inside.
redesign.interaction: Toggle past cone; drag a world line through P and see it turn red if it leaves the cone.

figures.label: Fig. 17.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: The flash in a spacetime diagram with two spatial dimensions dropped.
figures.visual_description: Horizontal x axis and vertical axis with marks t1, t2, t3. An inverted triangle has its vertex at P (height t1); horizontal chords at t2 and t3 show the front's extent, its sides being the 45 degree light rays.
figures.what_it_teaches: With two dimensions removed the light cone is a V of 45 degree lines, the form used for all subsequent Schwarzschild diagrams.

redesign.idea: Collapse animation that squashes the 3D cone of Fig. 17.5 onto the (t, x) plane, then relabels x as r, preparing learners for (t, r) diagrams in which each point is a sphere.
redesign.interaction: Button to flatten 3D to 2D; hover a point to see the 2-sphere it represents.

figures.label: Fig. 17.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Schwarzschild geometry drawn in Schwarzschild coordinates using radial light rays, with the angular dimensions suppressed.
figures.visual_description: Axes r (horizontal) and t (vertical). The t axis at r = 0 is a wavy line labelled Singularity; a vertical line marks r = 2m, with region II to its left and region I to its right. In region I, two families of curves cross: outgoing rays that rise from near r = 2m and bend toward 45 degrees, and ingoing rays descending from the upper right that steepen and hug r = 2m. Label arrows indicate 'Ingoing null congruence' (top) and 'Outgoing null congruence' (lower right). Small light cones sit at intersections: nearly 45 degree in I far out, very narrow near r = 2m, and in region II turned on their sides, opening toward the singularity.
figures.what_it_teaches: Shows cones narrowing to vertical slivers at r = 2m and tipping over inside, suggesting that infalling light and matter take infinite t to reach r = 2m; the authors flag the picture as misleading because I and II are disconnected charts.
concepts: regions I and II of Schwarzschild

redesign.idea: Chart comparison lab: the same set of radial null rays and an infalling particle plotted live in Schwarzschild (t, r) and in Eddington-Finkelstein (t-bar, r) side by side. A cursor at any event shows its light cone in both charts; the particle's world line is drawn in both, stalling at r = 2m on the left while crossing on the right.
redesign.interaction: Drag an event to place a light cone; slider for the family constant of ingoing/outgoing rays; toggle charts; play button for the infalling particle with a proper-time clock.

figures.label: Fig. 17.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: One radial infall described with the particle's own proper time and with Schwarzschild coordinate time.
figures.visual_description: Horizontal axis r with marks r = 0 (wavy vertical line), r = 2m (vertical line) and r = r0; vertical axis labelled t. From r0 at the bottom right, a curve labelled 'Proper time tau' rises gently and reaches r = 0 at finite height, passing r = 2m smoothly. A second curve labelled 'Coordinate time t' rises from r0 and bends upward to run asymptotically alongside r = 2m, never crossing.
figures.what_it_teaches: Makes vivid that proper time to the singularity is finite while Schwarzschild time diverges at the horizon: the divergence is a property of the clock/coordinate, not the particle.
concepts: exponential approach to the horizon in coordinate time

redesign.idea: Two-clock infall plot: the learner drops a probe from any r0 and sees tau(r) and t(r) computed from (17.15) and (17.17), with a Newtonian curve overlaid on tau. A zoom lens near r = 2m shows the exponential law on a log scale.
redesign.interaction: Slider for r0 (in units of m); toggle Newtonian overlay; log-scale toggle for r - 2m versus t; readout of tau to reach 2m and 0.

figures.label: Fig. 17.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Analytic extension: the coordinate range that works grows from region I alone to both regions.
figures.visual_description: Two side-by-side (r horizontal) quadrant diagrams joined by a double arrow. Left: vertical axis t, wavy axis at r = 0, vertical line at r = 2m; region I (right of the line) is hatched and labelled 'Coordinates good', region II is blank. Right: vertical axis t-bar, same line at r = 2m, but hatching now covers both II and I, with 'Coordinates good' pointing to both.
figures.what_it_teaches: The Eddington-Finkelstein metric is regular on a larger domain, so the spacetime can be enlarged across r = 2m.

redesign.idea: Patch overlap viewer: two coordinate patches shown as coloured regions on an abstract manifold strip, with their overlap highlighted; hovering in the overlap shows the same event's (t, r) and (t-bar, r) and the metric components in both, while hovering in II shows only the EF values and a 'Schwarzschild chart undefined' tag.
redesign.interaction: Hover to read coordinates and metric components; toggle to show the separate r < 2m map with ln(2m - r).

figures.label: Fig. 17.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Schwarzschild geometry in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates.
figures.visual_description: Axes r (horizontal) and t-bar (vertical), with the wavy t-bar axis at r = 0 labelled Singularity and a vertical line at r = 2m separating II (left) and I (right). Parallel straight lines at -45 degrees (labelled v = constant) are the ingoing rays. Curved outgoing rays in region I bend away from r = 2m toward the upper right; those in region II curve up and left into the singularity; the r = 2m line itself is a ray. Small light cones along the lines have one edge at -45 degrees and the other tilting: near 45 degrees far out, vertical on r = 2m, leaning inward in II. A dashed curve labelled 'Radially infalling particle' starts at the bottom in region I, rises up and to the left, crosses r = 2m about half way up without any kink, and ends on the singularity near the top of the axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: Light cones tilt continuously through the horizon, outgoing photons on r = 2m stay put, and an infalling particle crosses r = 2m smoothly and hits r = 0 in finite time.

redesign.idea: Light-cone field explorer in EF coordinates: a grid of cones whose shape is computed from (17.24); the learner drags a probe cone inward and watches its outer edge rotate to vertical at r = 2m and past it; launching photons or massive particles from the probe shows which reach infinity.
redesign.interaction: Drag probe event; buttons to fire outgoing/ingoing photons and a massive particle with chosen energy k; slider for mass m; toggle advanced/retarded chart.

figures.label: Fig. 17.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: Equatorial spatial picture of the Schwarzschild geometry in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates.
figures.visual_description: A large circle labelled r = 2m and, around its lower rim, 'ABSOLUTE EVENT HORIZON'; the inside is region II with an x at the centre labelled Singularity, the outside region I. Far outside, small circles have their emission dots at their centres. Near and on the horizon the small circles are displaced so the dot sits on their outer side (the circles touch or straddle r = 2m). Inside, the fronts are drawn as small cone/teardrop shapes pointing toward the central singularity.
figures.what_it_teaches: Wave fronts are increasingly dragged inward as r decreases; on r = 2m only the radially outward photon holds position and inside every front moves toward r = 0, so the horizon is a one-way membrane.

redesign.idea: Equatorial flash map: the learner places emitters anywhere in the plane around a black hole and watches each light front evolve for a short EF time step, computed from radial and non-radial null geodesics, with the fraction of the front that can still reach infinity shaded. Compared live with the flat-space panel (Fig. 17.3).
redesign.interaction: Click to place emitters; time-step slider; toggle 'escaping fraction' shading; side-by-side flat panel.

figures.label: Fig. 17.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Schwarzschild geometry in retarded Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates.
figures.visual_description: Axes r (horizontal) and t* (vertical), wavy axis at r = 0, vertical line at r = 2m separating II and I. Straight parallel lines at +45 degrees cross the whole diagram (outgoing rays, w = const). In region I, curves descend from the top near r = 2m and sweep down-right (ingoing rays that crowd against r = 2m toward the top); in region II, curves rise from the singularity axis and bend upward to hug r = 2m near the top. Small light cones are drawn along the lines.
figures.what_it_teaches: The mirror image in time of Fig. 17.10: outgoing rays are straight and r = 2m can be crossed only outward in the future, the white-hole extension.
concepts: time asymmetry of the Eddington-Finkelstein extension

redesign.idea: Time-reversal toggle on the Fig. 17.10 explorer: flipping t-bar -> -t* reflects the cones and ray families, and a counter shows which direction of crossing r = 2m is allowed in each chart.
redesign.interaction: Single toggle advanced/retarded with animated reflection; drag a probe to test crossings.

figures.label: Fig. 17.13
figures.caption_paraphrase: Spherical collapse of a star in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates with angular dimensions suppressed.
figures.visual_description: Axes r and t-bar. A hatched region at lower left labelled 'Star interior' is bounded by the star's surface world line, which curves up and left to meet the r = 0 axis; the axis below this is labelled 'Origin of polar coordinates' and above it is a wavy line labelled 'Singularity'. A dashed vertical line marks r = 2m (region II on the left, I on the right). A vertical line on the right is the 'World-line of distant observer'. Several curves leave the star surface and bend upward and to the right (signals at regular intervals); successive ones leave later, the ones emitted near r = 2m climb steeply, and the last are turned back into the singularity. Small tilted light cones are sketched in both regions.
figures.what_it_teaches: An observer on the star crosses r = 2m in finite time, but the signals reach the distant observer with growing delays; the signal from r = 2m stays there and later ones fall inward, so the star appears to freeze and then fades.

redesign.idea: Collapse and signals simulator: a star's surface follows a free-fall world line in EF coordinates; the learner sets the emission interval on the surface clock and sees null rays propagate to a distant observer, with a received-time readout and a spectrum/brightness bar that reddens and dims. The final ray at r = 2m and the trapped later rays are highlighted.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for initial radius and signal interval; play/pause; distant observer's received-signal timeline and brightness gauge; toggle to white-hole version (Exercise 17.17).

figures.label: Fig. 17.14
figures.caption_paraphrase: Collapse drawn in three dimensions (one spatial dimension suppressed).
figures.visual_description: A hatched bell-shaped solid labelled 'Star interior', wide at the bottom (dashed base ellipse) and narrowing upward to a point on the central axis. Where the shrinking star crosses a certain radius an ellipse marks the start of a dashed cylinder labelled 'Event horizon r = 2m'; the central axis above the apex is labelled 'Singularity'. Regions inside the cylinder are marked II, outside I; 'Empty space' labels the exterior. Small light cones scattered around tilt inward near and inside the cylinder and stand upright far away.
figures.what_it_teaches: The horizon is a tube in spacetime formed as the star passes 2m, with the singularity a line along the axis above the collapsed star; the 3D picture is Fig. 17.13 rotated about the time axis.

redesign.idea: Rotatable 3D collapse spacetime: the learner orbits a 2+1 rendering of the collapsing star, the horizon cylinder and light cones, and can drag a time slice upward to see the spatial snapshot (star radius, horizon circle) at that moment.
redesign.interaction: Orbit camera; time-slice slider; toggle light cones; highlight the horizon generator photons.

figures.label: Fig. 17.15
figures.caption_paraphrase: Newtonian escape from a uniform sphere.
figures.visual_description: A hatched disc of radius R with centre O; a radial line from O extends beyond the surface to a small particle of mass m at distance r, with an arrow v pointing radially outward.
figures.what_it_teaches: Sets up energy conservation for a radially escaping projectile, leading to the escape speed and the Newtonian critical radius.

redesign.idea: Escape-speed launcher: shrink a body at fixed mass and watch the escape speed grow until it reaches c at R = 2GM/c^2; launch corpuscles at speed c that rise and fall back when R is too small, contrasted with a relativistic panel where outgoing light at the horizon cannot rise at all.
redesign.interaction: Slider for R (or density at fixed R); launch button; side-by-side Newtonian and relativistic outcome.

figures.label: Fig. 17.16
figures.caption_paraphrase: Newtonian tides on a falling sphere of particles: before and after.
figures.visual_description: Two panels above a curved hatched surface labelled Earth. (a) A dotted circle labelled 'Sphere of particles' with a downward arrow. (b) Lower and closer to the Earth, a vertically elongated dotted oval labelled 'Ellipsoid of particles' with a downward arrow.
figures.what_it_teaches: Differential gravity stretches a falling cloud along the fall direction and squeezes it sideways, keeping its volume.

redesign.idea: Falling dust cloud: a ring of test particles released above a planet or black hole, integrated with the exact point-mass force (or geodesics), shows the cloud deforming; a readout compares the measured stretch and squeeze with 2m/r^3 and -m/r^3 and tracks area/volume.
redesign.interaction: Slider for central mass and release height; switch Newtonian/Schwarzschild; plot of axis ratio versus r.

figures.label: Fig. 17.17
figures.caption_paraphrase: An astronaut's body at successive stages of the plunge.
figures.visual_description: Three spacesuited figures from left to right: the first of normal proportions, the second somewhat taller and slimmer, the third markedly elongated and narrow, with a downward arrow beside it indicating the direction of fall.
figures.what_it_teaches: Radial stretching together with lateral compression grows without limit as the singularity is approached.

redesign.idea: Tidal-strain gauge for an infalling astronaut: choose black-hole mass and watch a stylized body stretched by the head-to-foot acceleration difference (2GM L / r^3 in physical units) as r falls; a marker shows where the strain exceeds human tolerance, which lies outside the horizon for stellar-mass holes and inside for supermassive ones.
redesign.interaction: Log slider for mass from 3 to 10^10 solar masses; play fall; readouts of tidal acceleration at the horizon and radius of lethal stretch.

figures.label: Fig. 17.18
figures.caption_paraphrase: A binary with an ordinary star feeding a black hole through an accretion disc.
figures.visual_description: Artist-style grey illustration: a large stippled sphere at right labelled 'Visible component' loses a stream of gas that arcs to the upper left into a flattened swirl labelled 'Accretion disc'; at its centre a dark spot is labelled 'Black hole', and several arrows radiate outward labelled 'X-rays'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Explains how a black hole in a binary can be detected by its mass (from the companion's orbit) and by X-rays from heated infalling gas.

redesign.idea: Binary mass-function explorer: the learner adjusts the visible star's radial-velocity curve (period, amplitude) and inclination and gets the minimum companion mass, colour-coded against white dwarf and neutron star limits; an animated accretion stream feeds a disc whose inner temperature sets the emitted X-ray energy.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for period, velocity amplitude, inclination, companion mass; live mass-function inequality; disc animation.

figures.label: Fig. 17.19
figures.caption_paraphrase: Asymmetries of a collapsing body are radiated away, leaving a symmetric end state.
figures.visual_description: Two hatched shapes. (a) A larger, nearly circular body with a bump on its upper-left edge labelled 'Asymmetry'. (b) A smaller, perfectly circular hatched disc.
figures.what_it_teaches: Perturbation analyses suggest a lumpy collapse settles to a spherical (Schwarzschild) black hole by radiating away its asymmetry.
concepts: no-hair relaxation of perturbed black holes

redesign.idea: Ringdown toy: a deformed horizon outline oscillates and relaxes to a circle with damped quadrupole modes, while a strain waveform plot shows the corresponding exponentially damped signal, linking to gravitational-wave ringdowns.
redesign.interaction: Slider for initial deformation amplitude and mode number; play; waveform panel.

worked_examples.problem: Determine the character and geometric meaning of each Schwarzschild coordinate.
worked_examples.method: Invert the diagonal metric (15.52) to get (17.2); read off signs for r > 2m; use t-independence and absence of cross terms to identify t as static world time; compute the induced metric on t, r constant to show sphere area 4 pi r^2; note the angles are fixed by spherical symmetry.
worked_examples.key_insight: Invariant properties (signs of g^aa, Killing symmetries, areas) rather than labels give coordinates their meaning, and they certify Schwarzschild's coordinates as canonical outside r = 2m.
worked_examples.result: t timelike and static time, r spacelike areal radius, theta and phi spacelike angles, for r > 2m; t and r swap character for r < 2m.

worked_examples.problem: Decide which of the places where the Schwarzschild metric degenerates are genuine singularities.
worked_examples.method: Treat the polar axis by switching to Cartesian coordinates; evaluate the chart-independent Kretschmann scalar 48 m^2/r^6 at r = 2m and r = 0.
